name: Urolithin A
lead: Urolithin A is a benzocoumarin compound formed when gut bacteria transform ellagic acid and ellagitannins, polyphenols found in pomegranates, walnuts, raspberries, strawberries and oak-aged wine [1]. It is not known to occur in any food itself, and how much a person produces depends on their gut microbiota, with efficiency varying widely and some individuals showing no conversion [1][2]. Supplements providing urolithin A directly are marketed for muscle and mitochondrial health in ageing, the best known being a branded form called Mitopure [3][4].

Urolithin A was identified in 2016 as a first-in-class natural compound that induces mitophagy, the clearance of damaged mitochondria, in worms and rodents [5]. Randomised trials in older and middle-aged adults have reported improvements in some muscle endurance and strength measures, along with safety and altered biomarkers, though effects on whole-body outcomes have been modest or mixed, and most trials were sponsored by the commercial supplier [3][6][7][8].
No published trial has tested urolithin A for facial or skin appearance. In training communities it is discussed as a mitochondrial and longevity supplement [9][10][11].

paras: Ellagitannins are hydrolysed in the gut to ellagic acid, which gut bacteria convert to urolithins through loss of a lactone and stepwise removal of hydroxyl groups. Gordonibacter species and Enterocloster species have been implicated, but the full set of organisms responsible is still unknown [1]. Studies of human metabolism describe three urolithin phenotypes, called metabotypes, which appear independent of food source, age and health status, so that some people are efficient producers and others produce little or none [2][13].

Once absorbed, urolithin A is conjugated in intestinal and liver cells and circulates mainly as glucuronide and sulfate forms before excretion in urine [1]. A 2022 review described 13 urolithins and their conjugates in the literature [14].

Urolithins were identified in human metabolism studies roughly two decades ago, and a Trends in Molecular Medicine review notes urolithin A was discovered around 40 years ago but only recently studied for ageing and disease [15][14]. A 2016 Nature Medicine paper reported that urolithin A induced mitophagy, prolonged lifespan in C. elegans and increased muscle function in rodents [5]. A 2019 Nature Metabolism paper described the first-in-human trial in healthy sedentary older adults, reporting a favourable safety profile and a molecular signature of improved mitochondrial health [7]. In 2018 the US FDA listed urolithin A as a safe ingredient for food products at 250 mg to 1 g per serving, according to Wikipedia [1].

Urolithin A is not marketed with an established appearance claim in the literature reviewed here; T Nation writers describe it as a longevity supplement and discuss muscle support in older lifters [16][11].

Human studies have examined muscle endurance in older adults, muscle strength in middle-aged adults and immune ageing [3][6][17]. Registered studies address COPD rehabilitation, glucose metabolism, obesity, frailty and Alzheimer's disease [18][19][20][21][22].

Urolithin A is proposed to stimulate mitophagy through the PINK1/Parkin pathway, clearing damaged mitochondria and improving mitochondrial function, and has been reported to reduce inflammation [12][15]. Animal studies report effects on gut barrier integrity through the Nrf2 pathway, on Alzheimer's disease models and on retinal neurodegeneration through lysophagy [23][24][25]. A 2025 review contrasted the roles of urolithin A and spermidine in mitophagy and autophagy [12].

A 2022 randomised placebo-controlled trial in middle-aged adults gave urolithin A (Mitopure) at two doses for 4 months and reported roughly 12 percent improvements in muscle strength along with changes in biomarkers of mitochondrial health [3]. A 2022 JAMA Network Open trial in older adults examined 6-minute walk distance, hand and leg muscle endurance and mitochondrial biomarkers [6]. A 2025 randomised trial in Nature Aging examined age-related immune decline [17].

A 2024 systematic review pooled five studies with 250 healthy individuals given 10 to 1,000 mg per day for 28 days to 4 months, and reported dose-dependent anti-inflammatory effects, changes in some mitochondrial genes and autophagy markers, no effect on maximal mitochondrial ATP production or gut microbiota composition, and increased muscle strength and endurance in some measures [8]. Several trials were sponsored by the supplement manufacturer [8][7].
Registered studies include bioavailability comparisons of different supplement formulations [4][26][27][28].

Wikipedia reports that in vivo studies found no specific toxicity from dietary urolithin A and that safety studies in older adults showed good tolerability, with mild side effects in preliminary human work [1]. The first-in-human trial reported a favourable safety profile at the doses tested [7]. Long-term safety data are limited.

On T Nation, users list Mitopure in pre-workout stacks, recommend it alongside NAD+, PQQ and fisetin for mitochondrial repair, and ask about cost, noting a branded product at over 110 dollars for 30 days [29][9][10]. A 77-year-old user reported taking urolithin A at 500 mg per day and later 1,000 mg per day with NAD+ and observing strength gains, which is anecdotal [11]. Site articles promote pomegranate punicalagins as precursors, describing sexual and cognitive health benefits [30][31].

lore.intro: Urolithin A is discussed in training forums as a mitochondrial repair supplement for muscle and ageing, often named in the same breath as NAD+ precursors and CoQ10 [9][10].

claims.claim: Urolithin A repairs mitochondria and improves muscle
claims.believers: Users cite podcasters and report strength gains on 500 to 1,000 mg per day [10][11].
claims.experts: Randomised trials report improved strength or endurance in some measures, while reviews note small samples and sponsor involvement [3][6][8].

claims.claim: Pomegranate or ellagitannin foods give the same benefit
claims.believers: T Nation articles promote pomegranate extracts and punicalagins as precursors [32][30].
claims.experts: Conversion depends on gut microbiota, and some people produce little or no urolithin A [1][2].

claims.claim: It improves sexual health and brain function
claims.believers: Articles attribute improved blood flow, learning and memory to punicalagin-derived urolithin A [30][31].
claims.experts: Preclinical Alzheimer's models show effects, but no cited human trial establishes sexual or cognitive benefit [24].
